documents.unit: Martha Bradley Evans Center for Teaching Excellence
documents.title: Fall 2023 Instructional Guidelines on generative AI
documents.summary: A 2023 teaching-center post for instructors that recommends a syllabus statement tying unauthorized or uncited AI use to academic misconduct and suggests assignment redesigns. It also points to detectors, with a caution about Turnitin, and to faculty learning events. It sets no AI rule for courses itself.
documents.stance_why: The post only 'recommends that all faculty include a statement on their syllabus' and suggests strategies; it never allows or bans AI for any work and leaves course rules to instructors, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The Center 'recommends that all faculty include a statement on their syllabus' about AI misrepresentation, so it asks instructors to put an AI statement in the syllabus: an instructor action at course start, a recommendation (should), type P09.
units.anchor: recommends that all faculty include a statement on their syllabus

units.why: The suggested statement says AI use 'without citation, documentation, or authorization' falls under academic honesty rules; it classes unauthorized AI use as a breach of academic honesty, so P36, binding students.
units.anchor: This includes the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools without citation, documentation, or authorization.

units.why: The same sentence makes citation or documentation the condition for AI use: tools used 'without citation, documentation, or authorization' are a violation, so students are expected to cite or document AI use. Coded P24 (disclosure) in addition to the misconduct unit; the misconduct label is the P36 unit above.
units.anchor: without citation, documentation, or authorization
units.policy: Students cite or document their use of generative AI tools, or have authorization for it.
units.fit_note: Also covers 'authorization' as an alternative to citation, which P24 does not capture.

units.why: The statement asks students to 'adhere to the prescribed professional and ethical standards of the profession/discipline'; this is a general call to responsible conduct with no AI-specific content, so P116.
units.anchor: Students are expected to adhere to the prescribed professional and ethical standards of the profession/discipline
units.fit_note: Ties conduct to the norms of the student's profession or discipline.

units.why: Violators 'may be subject to academic sanctions as per the University of Utah's Student Code', so misuse falls under existing university conduct policy rather than a new AI rule: P77.
units.anchor: may be subject to academic sanctions as per the University of Utah’s Student Code

units.why: The guidance recommends 'assignments that require students to do more than just produce an answer', i.e. redesigning take-home work around AI; this is instructor-facing assessment design (P35).
units.anchor: we recommend using assignments that require students to do more than just produce an answer

units.why: It suggests students 'respond in an alternative format, such as creating a video response or a poster presentation', another assignment redesign aimed at AI, so P35.
units.anchor: they may be asked to respond in an alternative format, such as creating a video

units.why: 'Requiring students to include citations or documentation in a manner that would be difficult for an AI generator is another strategy we suggest' is an assignment-design response to AI, so P35.
units.anchor: Requiring students to include citations or documentation in a manner that would be difficult for

units.why: 'Familiarize yourself with popular AI tools and the kinds of responses they may produce' tells instructors to learn about AI tools before setting policy, which is faculty support (P63) rather than a student rule.
units.anchor: Familiarize yourself with popular AI tools and the kinds of responses they may produce to

units.why: Canvas 'is equipped with Turnitin... that also produces an AI Originality score'; this describes a detection tool available to instructors, so it is a similarity/AI-detection tool unit (P40) stated as fact.
units.anchor: Canvas is equipped with Turnitin, a plagiarism tool, that also produces an AI Originality score

units.why: MBECTE 'recommended that faculty not rely on Turnitin's Originality score to detect all AI usage due to reported reliability issues', which is a caution against relying on a detector (P39), not a ban.
units.anchor: recommended that faculty not rely on Turnitin’s Originality score to detect all AI usage

units.why: 'Faculty are encouraged to explore independent AI detection tools, such as ZeroGPT, or Writer' recommends using detectors to identify AI use (P40); it pulls the other way from the Turnitin caution in the same section.
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to explore independent AI detection tools

units.why: 'We encourage you to attend talks on AI and stay updated on the latest developments' asks faculty to keep learning, which is faculty support through events (P63); the explicit 'stay informed' unit is coded separately.
units.anchor: We encourage you to attend talks on AI and stay updated on the latest developments.

units.why: 'MBECTE will also hold a campuswide workshop on AI and Writing' announces a workshop for faculty, graduate students and staff: faculty support through workshops (P63).
units.anchor: MBECTE will also hold a campuswide workshop on AI and Writing on November 30.

units.why: 'We recommend faculty stay abreast of developments in their own field' is a duty to keep up with AI developments, which matches P102.
units.anchor: we recommend faculty stay abreast of developments in their own field

units.why: 'Level up with self-paced courses on AI' points faculty to self-paced AI courses and a micro bootcamp: support for faculty learning (P63).
units.anchor: Level up with self-paced courses on AI.

units.why: 'The MBECTE Team is excited about the possibilities that generative AI brings to higher education teaching practices' states a positive view of AI for teaching without a rule, closest to P87 (benefits).
units.anchor: excited about the possibilities that generative AI brings to higher education teaching practices
units.fit_note: A general statement of enthusiasm; no specific benefit is named.

documents.title: Gen AI Acceptable Use - AI & You Student Guide
tiers: Level 3 AI for Specified Task Completion
Level 4 Full AI Use with Human Oversight
Level 5 Full AI Use without Human Oversight
documents.summary: A student-facing guide with a six-level scale of AI use, each level with a description, disclosure standard and examples. Instructors choose the level per assignment. It requires APA citation at Levels 3 and 4 and treats undisclosed required AI use as academic misconduct.
documents.stance_why: The guide offers a tiered scale and says 'Instructors will communicate the level of AI use permitted for each assignment' and 'may set different AI use levels for different assignments', so it sets no stance itself and lists tiers: delegates.

units.why: 'Instructors will communicate the level of AI use permitted for each assignment' puts the duty on instructors to state expectations per assignment at the start of the work: a communication rule (P09), with the per-assignment variation coded as P04 below.
units.anchor: Instructors will communicate the level of AI use permitted for each assignment.

units.why: The guide sorts AI use into 'Level 0 AI Usage' through 'Level 5 AI Usage', named levels from No AI Use to Full AI Use without Human Oversight, which is the definition of P05 (named tiers).
units.anchor: Level 0 AI Usage No AI Use
units.policy: AI use is sorted into six levels: Level 0 No AI Use, Level 1 AI-Assisted Editing, Level 2 AI-Assisted Structuring & Searching, Level 3 AI for Specified Task Completion, Level 4 Full AI Use with Human Oversight, Level 5 Full AI Use without Human Oversight.

units.why: 'This scale applies to tools such as ChatGPT EDU, Gemini, Copilot, image generators, and other AI tools that create new content' defines which AI the scale covers: scope definition, P61.
units.anchor: This scale applies to tools such as ChatGPT EDU, Gemini, Copilot, image generators

units.why: 'Students are encouraged to use university-approved AI tools' asks students to prefer licensed tools; it is an institution-wide recommendation (P92), not a single course's tool (P17).
units.anchor: Students are encouraged to use university-approved AI tools

units.why: The approved tools are preferred 'because they provide enhanced security and data protections through the university's enterprise agreement'; this is the privacy reason for the preference, so P50.
units.anchor: enhanced security and data protections through the university’s enterprise agreement

units.why: 'Questions about permitted AI use should be directed to the instructor, mentor, or adviser' tells students to ask when unsure, so P10 (it also mentions the syllabus, covered by the next unit).
units.anchor: Questions about permitted AI use should be directed to the instructor, mentor, or adviser

units.why: 'Always check your specific course syllabus' makes students responsible for finding each course's AI rules, which is P78 (distinct from P10, which is asking when unsure).
units.anchor: Always check your specific course syllabus.

units.why: 'Instructors may set different AI use levels for different assignments within the same course' lets the level vary by assignment, so the rule is set per assignment: P04.
units.anchor: Instructors may set different AI use levels for different assignments within the same course.

units.why: Students 'should be able to explain to your instructor/mentor/adviser how you used AI and why you made the choices you did'; the closest type is P30 (explain and defend what you submit), though it asks to explain AI use rather than every line.
units.anchor: you should be able to explain to your instructor/mentor/adviser how you used AI and why
units.fit_note: Asks students to explain how and why they used AI, beyond citing it, not to explain every line of submitted work.

units.why: Level 0 says 'The assignment is completed entirely on your own, without any AI assistance', a ban on AI for the assignment, so P01 (prohibit by default for that assignment type).
units.anchor: The assignment is completed entirely on your own, without any AI assistance.
units.fit_note: A prohibition at one level of the scale, not a default for the whole course.

units.why: The Level 0 examples are a proctored 'Closed-book problem-solving exam ... with no devices allowed', an in-person assessment with no AI: P22 (stated as an example, so informs).
units.anchor: Closed-book problem-solving exam in an introductory calculus course, proctored in person with no devices allowed.

units.why: 'No AI disclosure is required' at Level 0 says no disclosure applies because no AI is used; it is a disclosure rule (P24), stated as a condition of the level.
units.anchor: No AI disclosure is required.
units.policy: At Level 0, no AI disclosure is required.
units.fit_note: States that disclosure is not required at this level; P24 is about requiring it.

units.why: Level 1 lets students 'use AI to help refine, debug, translate, and/or polish' content they wrote themselves: AI allowed for editing and writing support (P91).
units.anchor: You write the content yourself, then use AI to help refine, debug, translate, and/or polish

units.why: Level 1 adds that AI 'should not generate new content for you', which bars AI-generated submitted content at that level: P19.
units.anchor: should not generate new content for you

units.why: Level 1 disclosure is 'No disclosure, unless specified', so edit-level AI use needs no disclosure by default: P24 with a fit note since it says disclosure is not required.
units.anchor: No disclosure, unless specified. Draft of a lab report where you write methods
units.policy: At Level 1, no disclosure is required unless specified.
units.fit_note: States that disclosure is not required (unless specified), not that it is required.

units.why: The Level 1 example 'You ask AI to help suggest a bug fix' for code that does not compile is permitted debugging help, P13.
units.anchor: Your code for a programming assignment does not compile. You ask AI to help suggest

units.why: The same example requires the student to 'still verify on your own that the program satisfies the specifications', so the student must check AI output: P31.
units.anchor: still verify on your own that the program satisfies the specifications

units.why: Level 2 lets students 'use AI to help brainstorm, build outlines, search for tools, explain concepts, and generate ideas', a permission for brainstorming and structuring: P15.
units.anchor: use AI to help brainstorm, build outlines, search for tools, explain concepts, and generate ideas
units.fit_note: Also covers explaining concepts and searching for tools, beyond brainstorming.

units.why: 'the actual content you submit is your own' limits Level 2 so AI cannot be the author of what is submitted; the student owns the submission (P29).
units.anchor: the actual content you submit is your own

units.why: Level 2 disclosure is 'No disclosure, unless specified. The material generated is your own', so again disclosure is not required by default: P24 with a fit note.
units.anchor: No disclosure, unless specified. The material generated is your own.
units.policy: At Level 2, no disclosure is required unless specified, because the material generated is the student's own.
units.fit_note: States that disclosure is not required, not that it is required.

units.why: The Level 2 discussion-board example says students 'must write and post your own response in Canvas', so AI may inspire but not produce the post: P19.
units.anchor: must write and post your own response in Canvas

units.why: The example of searching 'for a Python library call to solve a particular step... but you implement the function' allows AI as a search aid for code while the student writes the function: P12 (search or tutor use), with a fit note.
units.anchor: you implement the function within the assignment context
units.fit_note: AI is used to find a library call and an example, not to understand concepts.

units.why: An international student may use AI 'to translate work from their native language into English', a prose-support use allowed at Level 2: P18 (prose rule separate from code).
units.anchor: An international student uses generative AI to translate work from their native language into English

units.why: Level 3 lets students 'use AI to complete and generate content that may be used verbatim or lightly edited', which permits AI-generated submitted content under conditions: P16.
units.anchor: You use AI to complete and generate content that may be used verbatim or lightly

units.why: Level 3 says the 'student is expected to think critically about what AI produces and take responsibility for reviewing and evaluating all AI-generated content', a duty to verify output: P31.
units.anchor: take responsibility for reviewing and evaluating all AI-generated content

units.why: 'AI-created content must be cited using proper APA style. Include an in-text citation and reference entry' requires citation with the submission: P24.
units.anchor: AI-created content must be cited using proper APA style.

units.why: 'links to AI chat(s) may be submitted with the submission' depending on the course means instructors may ask for chat logs: P26, with modality may because it is conditional.
units.anchor: links to AI chat(s) may be submitted with the submission

units.why: The Level 3 example has students 'explicitly told to use AI to generate three alternative ad copy drafts', an assignment that requires AI use: P79.
units.anchor: you are explicitly told to use AI to generate three alternative ad copy drafts for

units.why: In the Level 3 computing example a student uses 'an AI coding assistant to generate or autocomplete a small function' while completing the design and checking the system: allowed AI-generated code under a condition, P16 (an editor-integrated assistant also appears, but the unit is the small-function allowance).
units.anchor: they use an AI coding assistant to generate or autocomplete a small function

units.why: Level 4 describes students using AI 'freely throughout the assignment as a co-pilot', which allows broad AI use: P02.
units.anchor: A student uses AI freely throughout the assignment as a co-pilot to support their work.

units.why: 'The key responsibility is the human review of everything AI produces, ensuring accuracy' makes the student verify all AI output at Level 4: P31.
units.anchor: The key responsibility is the human review of everything AI produces, ensuring accuracy
units.fit_note: Also says the final product must reflect the student's own judgment and understanding.

units.why: 'You must cite all uses of AI using APA style, including in-text citations and reference entries' is a Level 4 citation rule, P24.
units.anchor: You must cite all uses of AI using APA style, including in-text citations and reference

units.why: The Level 4 design-studio example ends with 'submitting an AI use log and critical reflection', a log and reflection submitted with the work: P26.
units.anchor: combined with submitting an AI use log and critical reflection

units.why: An engineer 'uses an advanced coding agent, such as ChatGPT Codex, to generate software for a complex project', so coding agents are allowed at Level 4: P07.
units.anchor: uses an advanced coding agent, such as ChatGPT Codex, to generate software for a complex
units.fit_note: Describes a permitted use of an autonomous coding agent; the type is mainly about rules for embedded tools and agents.

units.why: The same example ends with 'including turning in their chat prompt logs', so prompt logs are submitted with the report: P26.
units.anchor: including turning in their chat prompt logs

units.why: Level 5 is where 'Students fully delegate academic judgment, grading decisions, research authorship, or evaluative responsibilities to AI without meaningful review or understanding', which the guide treats as the unacceptable end of the scale: P32 (students must stay the thinkers).
units.anchor: Students fully delegate academic judgment, grading decisions, research authorship, or evaluative responsibilities to AI

units.why: 'Failure to disclose required AI use or delegating academic judgment to AI may constitute academic misconduct and/or research misconduct' classes these acts as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: may constitute academic misconduct and/or research misconduct

units.why: 'Posting AI-generated discussion posts in Canvas without review or disclosure' is listed as an example of Level 5 misuse, so posting unreviewed, undisclosed AI text is barred: P24 (disclosure), with the missing review noted.
units.anchor: Posting AI-generated discussion posts in Canvas without review or disclosure.
units.fit_note: Also bars posting AI text that the student has not reviewed.

units.why: 'Generating an AI summary of an article for an assignment submission without review or disclosure' is a Level 5 example, so using AI summaries without review or disclosure is barred: P24, with the missing review noted.
units.anchor: Generating an AI summary of an article for an assignment submission without review or disclosure.
units.fit_note: Also bars using an AI summary that the student has not reviewed.

units.why: 'Generating code using a generative AI tool for an assignment that states that this assignment shall not use AI' is Level 5 misuse: AI-generated code where the assignment forbids AI, P19.
units.anchor: Generating code using a generative AI tool for an assignment that states that this assignment

units.why: 'If you use AI and do not disclose it when required, it is considered Academic Misconduct and will be handled in accordance with Policy 6-410' makes nondisclosure the violation: P28.
units.anchor: If you use AI and do not disclose it when required, it is considered Academic

units.why: 'Whenever AI plays a meaningful role in your work, you should disclose and cite it' sets a general disclosure expectation with a materiality threshold: P24.
units.anchor: Whenever AI plays a meaningful role in your work, you should disclose and cite it.

units.why: The disclosure template asks for '(tool name, model/version, date)' and the purpose of use, so disclosures name the tool, model and date: P25.
units.anchor: This assignment used generative AI (tool name, model/version, date)
units.fit_note: A template statement; it also names the purpose of the AI use.

units.why: The 'APA Reference Format' gives 'Author of AI tool. (Year). Name of AI tool (Version) [Type of AI model]. URL' as the University's recommended baseline citation form: P25.
units.anchor: Author of AI tool. (Year). Name of AI tool (Version) [Type of AI model]. URL

units.why: 'When citing AI-generated content in your text (Levels 3-4), use: (OpenAI, 2026)' tells students the in-text citation form for Levels 3 and 4: P24.
units.anchor: When citing AI-generated content in your text (Levels 3–4), use: (OpenAI, 2026)

units.why: 'Adapted from: Perkins, Furze, et al. (2024). The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)' states which published framework the levels were adapted from, so it describes how the guide was made: P84.
units.anchor: Adapted from: Perkins, M., Furze, L., et al. (2024). The AI Assessment Scale (AIAS)
units.fit_note: Names source frameworks (AIAS, Frostburg State, TESOL) only; no process or date of adoption is given.

documents.title: AI Tools for Education
documents.summary: A long CTE resource page for instructors on teaching with AI. It recommends a syllabus statement, clear course-level AI rules, citation, privacy limits, and equity, and says to avoid AI detectors. It sets conditions for AI-assisted grading and describes campus AI tools such as UBot. It leaves course-level AI permissions to instructors.
documents.stance_why: The page advises instructors to 'clearly state if, when, and how generative AI may be used' and says 'there's no universal standard', so it sets no allow-or-ban rule for students and hands the decision to instructors: delegates.

units.why: 'Learn more about the University of Utah's approved AI tools and AI Policies and Guidelines' sends readers to other university guidance: P115.
units.anchor: Learn more about the University of Utah’s approved AI tools

units.why: '73% of employers use GenAI while more than half (55%) of graduates said their program did not prepare them' is cited to argue that students need AI skills for work: P44.
units.anchor: 73% of employers use GenAI while more than half (55%) of graduates said their program

units.why: 'this page offers strategies, examples, and resources to guide your teaching practice' describes the page as support for instructors learning to teach with AI: P63.
units.anchor: this page offers strategies, examples, and resources to guide your teaching practice

units.why: 'AI technologies power adaptive learning systems that tailor instruction to individual student needs, increasing engagement and promoting deeper learning' names benefits of AI for learning without making a rule: P87.
units.anchor: AI technologies power adaptive learning systems that tailor instruction to individual student needs

units.why: 'Ethical challenges—such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, intellectual property rights, and the potential commercialization of education' lists harms to be handled with care: P53.
units.anchor: Ethical challenges—such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, intellectual property rights, and the potential commercialization of

units.why: 'moving beyond awareness to active engagement with AI tools in order to prepare students for a workforce that already demands AI literacy' tells faculty to engage with AI for career reasons: P44.
units.anchor: moving beyond awareness to active engagement with AI tools in order to prepare students for

units.why: 'We are committed to supporting instructors in developing the digital competencies, reflective practices, and instructional strategies needed to use AI' is a commitment of faculty support: P63.
units.anchor: We are committed to supporting instructors in developing the digital competencies, reflective practices, and instructional

units.why: 'Rather than banning or ignoring AI, educators can design learning experiences that leverage its strengths' favors integrating AI over banning it: P02 (permit or encourage), with a fit note since it is advice rather than a default rule.
units.anchor: Rather than banning or ignoring AI, educators can design learning experiences that leverage its strengths
units.fit_note: Advice to instructors to integrate AI rather than ban it, not a rule about what students may do.

units.why: 'Begin your course with an open discussion about AI' tells instructors to talk with students about AI at the start: P66.
units.anchor: Begin your course with an open discussion about AI.

units.why: 'Frame AI as a professional skill and ethical responsibility' asks instructors to present AI as a professional skill: P44.
units.anchor: Frame AI as a professional skill and ethical responsibility.

units.why: 'Use assignments that require analysis, synthesis, and evaluation—not just recall' recommends redesigning assignments for AI: P35.
units.anchor: Use assignments that require analysis, synthesis, and evaluation—not just recall.

units.why: 'Use the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) to establish appropriate criteria for success for assessments' points instructors to a named scale of AI levels: P05.
units.anchor: Use the AI Assessment Scale (AIAS) to establish appropriate criteria for success for assessments.
units.fit_note: Recommends adopting an external scale; no levels are listed on this page.

units.why: 'Ask students to reflect on how they used AI in an assignment' recommends reflections on AI use, and says to include them in the grade: P26.
units.anchor: Ask students to reflect on how they used AI in an assignment

units.why: 'Consider giving students the option to complete assignments with or without AI tools' offers AI-assisted and AI-free versions of assignments, a redesign around AI: P35.
units.anchor: Consider giving students the option to complete assignments with or without AI tools.
units.fit_note: Offers parallel AI-assisted and AI-free versions as a design choice.

units.why: The heading '5. Ditch Detection Tools' tells instructors not to use AI detectors, so P39 (do not rely on detectors) applies.
units.anchor: 5. Ditch Detection Tools
units.policy: Instructors should not use AI-detection tools.

units.why: 'AI-detection tools have repeatedly proven to be unreliable and inaccurate, often yielding false alarms flagging student work' gives the reason detectors are not relied on: P39.
units.anchor: AI-detection tools have repeatedly proven to be unreliable and inaccurate

units.why: Detectors 'could expose FERPA-secured data to significant security risks' gives a privacy reason against detectors: P50.
units.anchor: could expose FERPA-secured data to significant security risks

units.why: Detectors 'are not on the list of UIT-approved AI tools', so they fall outside the university's approved tools: P92.
units.anchor: They are not on the list of UIT-approved AI tools
units.fit_note: Used as a reason against detectors, not as a general rule to use approved tools.

units.why: 'prevent misuse by designing clear, specific, and creative tasks—then emphasize honest communication and trust' proposes task design as the alternative to detection: P35.
units.anchor: prevent misuse by designing clear, specific, and creative tasks

units.why: 'you have a duty to your students to ensure their information is protected' states the instructor's data duty when using AI: P50.
units.anchor: As an instructor, you have a duty to your students to ensure their information is

units.why: 'Never enter or upload sensitive or restricted data per Rule 4-004C' forbids entering sensitive data (PHI, FERPA, PII) into AI tools: P50.
units.anchor: Never enter or upload sensitive or restricted data

units.why: 'You may choose to anonymize your data for use with AI tools' allows anonymizing data before use: P50 (protect personal data).
units.anchor: You may choose to anonymize

units.why: 'Any intellectual property belonging to students, staff, or faculty should not be input without explicit consent' restricts inputting others' IP into AI: P52 (ownership of AI inputs), with a fit note.
units.anchor: should not be input without explicit consent
units.fit_note: Concerns consent before inputting others' IP into AI, not licensing or copyright of output.

units.why: 'When in doubt, contact UIT or the U of U Automation Center of Excellence' points instructors to offices for help on AI data questions: P115.
units.anchor: When in doubt, contact UIT or the U of U Automation Center of Excellence (ACoE)

units.why: 'we highly recommend using Microsoft Copilot over other generative AI tools like ChatGPT' recommends a university-provided tool for data protection: P92.
units.anchor: we highly recommend using Microsoft Copilot over other generative AI tools like ChatGPT

units.why: Even Copilot 'sensitive or restricted data ... should never be shared through Microsoft Copilot chat' restates the data limit for the recommended tool: P50.
units.anchor: should never be shared through Microsoft Copilot chat

units.why: 'using Microsoft Copilot for patient-related activity is prohibited' bans Copilot for patient information at University of Utah Health: P50 (protect confidential data).
units.anchor: using Microsoft Copilot for patient-related activity is prohibited

units.why: 'Chats with Copilot are not added to the OpenAI language model database' states how the university-licensed tool handles data: P50.
units.anchor: Chats with Copilot are not added to the OpenAI language model database.

units.why: 'It is critical to verify that the green shield is present for all conversations' tells users to check that the protected mode is on: P50.
units.anchor: It is critical to verify that the green shield is present for all conversations.

units.why: 'We highly recommend including a statement in your syllabus detailing expectations around use of generative AI tools' asks instructors to put an AI statement in the syllabus: P09.
units.anchor: We highly recommend including a statement in your syllabus detailing expectations around use of generative

units.why: The sample statement says AI use 'without citation, documentation, or authorization' is covered by academic honesty rules, classing unauthorized AI use as an honesty breach: P36.
units.anchor: This includes the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools without citation, documentation, or authorization.

units.why: The sample statement says violators 'may be subject to academic sanctions as per Policy 6-410', so sanctions come through existing university policy: P77.
units.anchor: may be subject to academic sanctions as per Policy 6-410

units.why: 'You are free to use and edit the statement listed above' lets instructors adopt and adapt the supplied syllabus language: P110.
units.anchor: You are free to use and edit the statement listed above.

units.why: 'Find other optional syllabus additions available from CTE' directs instructors to further CTE syllabus language: P110.
units.anchor: Find other optional syllabus additions available from CTE.

units.why: 'Some departments may elect to create a broad AI policy for all courses in their department' says units may set their own AI rules: P85.
units.anchor: Some departments may elect to create a broad AI policy for all courses in their

units.why: 'Take a look at a sample department AI use statement from Writing and Rhetoric Studies' offers a sample statement: P110.
units.anchor: sample department AI use statement from Writing and Rhetoric Studies

units.why: 'Because there's no universal standard for AI use in education, instructors must proactively guide students by setting clear boundaries' leaves the rule to each instructor: P04.
units.anchor: instructors must proactively guide students by setting clear boundaries, explaining appropriate use, and adapting policies
units.fit_note: Also asks instructors to explain appropriate use and adapt policies.

units.why: 'In course syllabus and assignment instructions, instructors should clearly state if, when, and how generative AI may be used' requires stating AI expectations in the syllabus and assignments: P09.
units.anchor: instructors should clearly state if, when, and how generative AI may be used

units.why: 'acceptable use cases (e.g. brainstorming ideas, improving grammar, changing linguistic style)' gives examples of allowed uses: P15, noting that grammar and style help also appears.
units.anchor: acceptable use cases (e.g. brainstorming ideas, improving grammar, changing linguistic style)
units.fit_note: Also names grammar and style editing as examples of acceptable use.

units.why: 'prohibited uses (e.g. submitting AI-generated text as one's own work)' gives the example prohibited use, so P19.
units.anchor: prohibited uses (e.g. submitting AI-generated text as one’s own work)

units.why: 'Use CTE's Student Guide to AI Generative Tools to set classroom norms' points instructors to the student guide: P115.
units.anchor: Use CTE’s Student Guide to AI Generative Tools to set classroom norms.

units.why: 'Clear distinction should be made between legitimate assistance and cheating. Examples of both can help students understand' asks instructors to explain the line with examples: P66.
units.anchor: Clear distinction should be made between legitimate assistance and cheating.
units.fit_note: Asks for examples of both legitimate assistance and cheating.

units.why: 'no universal standard for what counts as "AI plagiarism" and no foolproof detection method for AI-generated content' says misuse cannot be fully identified or defined: P82.
units.anchor: no foolproof detection method for AI-generated content

units.why: 'instructors might allow AI-generated support for researching a problem and potential solutions' gives an example of allowed AI help in research: P12 (AI as a search or tutor aid).
units.anchor: instructors might allow AI-generated support for researching a problem and potential solutions
units.fit_note: Describes AI for researching a problem and solutions rather than explaining concepts.

units.why: 'but not for writing entire case analyses' gives the matching example of a barred use, AI writing the whole submission: P19.
units.anchor: but not for writing entire case analyses

units.why: 'Here is an example policy that balances faculty independence with shared expectations' links to a sample policy: P110.
units.anchor: Here is an example policy that balances faculty independence with shared expectations.

units.why: 'Treat AI outputs like any other source that students must cite' puts AI under existing source and citation rules: P45.
units.anchor: Treat AI outputs like any other source that students must cite.

units.why: 'require them to openly acknowledge how they used it' asks instructors to require students to acknowledge AI use: P24.
units.anchor: require them to openly acknowledge how they used it

units.why: 'Prompts, any direct text or data from an AI model should be quoted or cited, and paraphrased AI content should be attributed as well' names the prompt and the output as items to cite: P25.

units.why: 'should not be input into public AI tools' limits what students enter into public AI tools, with sensitive and confidential information as the case: P50.

units.why: 'Students should understand that AI models can exhibit biases, make up information, or reflect limited perspectives' names bias and invented content as harms: P53.

units.why: 'Instructors and DESB should treat AI usage policies as living documents' says policies will change and should be revisited, and invites student feedback: P54.

units.why: 'Instructors should be prepared to adjust guidelines each semester' sets a revision expectation for course policies: P54.

units.why: 'Instructors could start with a low-stakes or ungraded activity to let students get hands-on experience' introduces AI gradually: P70 (student AI literacy).
units.anchor: Instructors could start with a low-stakes or ungraded activity to let students get hands-on experience.

units.why: 'Dedicating some class time to explaining how generative AI works in general terms and what its limitations are' asks for AI literacy teaching: P70.

units.why: 'large language models predict text based on patterns – they do not "think" or verify facts' says AI output may be unverified, so users must check it: P31.

units.why: 'Creating a classroom culture where students can openly discuss their experiences with AI' asks for open class dialogue on AI: P66.

units.why: 'Effective use of AI in coursework should always serve your learning objectives—not override them' ties AI decisions to learning goals: P83.
units.anchor: Effective use of AI in coursework should always serve your learning objectives—not override them.

units.why: 'the analysis and final decision must be entirely their own' keeps the student as the decision-maker when AI gathers data or options: P32.

units.why: 'Break complex assignments into a series of smaller steps or milestones' recommends staged submissions: P35.
units.anchor: Break complex assignments into a series of smaller steps or milestones.

units.anchor: never take AI output at face value without oversight and verification

units.anchor: strongly discourages the use of artificial intelligence tools to determine or assign student grades

documents.title: Plagiarism & AI Policies
documents.summary: The ECE department's plagiarism and AI page. Coursework AI use is left to the instructor and the syllabus; research AI use goes to the supervisory committee chair, the VP of Research and journal rules. It quotes arXiv and IEEE guidance on author responsibility and disclosure.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'The allowed or disallowed use of AI in coursework will be at the discretion of the instructor' and sends research use to the committee chair, so it sets no stance of its own: delegates.

units.why: 'Plagiarism is a serious academic and research misconduct offense' states how the department classes plagiarism: P36 (misconduct), without naming AI here.
units.anchor: Plagiarism is a serious academic and research misconduct offense.
units.fit_note: Plagiarism in general; AI is not named in this sentence.

units.why: 'Reports of Research Misconduct, including plagiarism, should be made to the Office of Research Integrity and Compliance' gives the reporting channel for research misconduct: P81.
units.anchor: Reports of Research Misconduct, including plagiarism, should be made to the

units.why: 'Reports of academic misconduct should be made to the instructor of the course..., the ECE Department Chair, and the Associate Dean' gives the reporting channel for coursework misconduct: P81.
units.anchor: Reports of academic misconduct should be made to the instructor of the course

units.why: 'A student may report to any one of these, who will then inform the others of the report' sets how reports are routed: P81.
units.anchor: A student may report to any one of these, who will then inform the others

units.why: 'policies and practices related to AI are quickly evolving' says the policy is provisional: P54.
units.anchor: policies and practices related to AI are quickly evolving

units.why: 'As new policies are developed at the university, college, or department level, ECE will also adhere to those policies' commits the department to follow higher-level AI policy: P77 (comply with university policy).
units.anchor: ECE will also adhere to those policies
units.fit_note: A department commits to follow future university and college AI policies.

units.why: 'use of AI in coursework will be at the discretion of the instructor' leaves the rule to each instructor: P04.
units.anchor: use of AI in coursework will be at the discretion of the instructor

units.why: 'and should be posted in the course syllabus' requires the instructor's AI rule to be in the syllabus: P09.
units.anchor: and should be posted in the course syllabus

units.why: 'The use of AI in research will be at the discretion of the student's supervisory committee chair' sets who decides AI use in research: P62.
units.anchor: The use of AI in research will be at the discretion of the student’s supervisory

units.why: 'The use should conform to expectations set out by the VP of Research' makes AI in research follow a higher-level body's rules: P62.
units.anchor: The use should conform to

units.why: 'The use of AI in research writing/publication should follow the guidance and policies of the journal' defers to venue rules: P62.
units.anchor: should follow the guidance and policies of the journal for which the writing is being

units.why: 'should be discussed with the student's supervisory committee chair' asks students to talk to their chair about AI in research writing: P62.
units.anchor: should be discussed with the student’s supervisory committee chair

units.why: 'NOT acknowledging the use of AI in research, writing, editing, etc. can be considered plagiarism' makes nondisclosure the violation: P28.
units.anchor: NOT acknowledging the use of AI in research, writing, editing, etc. can be considered plagiarism.

units.why: The arXiv excerpt says authors 'take full responsibility for all its contents, irrespective of how the contents were generated': authors own what they submit, P29.
units.anchor: take full responsibility for all its contents, irrespective of how the contents were generated

units.why: 'If generative AI language tools generate inappropriate language, plagiarized content, errors... it is the responsibility of the author(s)' says AI errors and plagiarism are the author's problem, so output must be checked: P31.
units.anchor: it is the responsibility of the author(s)
units.fit_note: Assigns responsibility for AI errors and plagiarism to the author.

units.why: IEEE guidance says AI-generated content 'shall be disclosed in the acknowledgments section of any article submitted to an IEEE publication', a disclosure rule: P24.
units.anchor: shall be disclosed in the acknowledgments section of any article submitted to an IEEE publication
units.fit_note: Applies to articles submitted to IEEE publications and covers text, figures, images and code.

units.why: 'The AI system used shall be identified' requires naming the tool in the disclosure: P25.
units.anchor: The AI system used shall be identified

units.why: 'specific sections of the article that use AI-generated content shall be identified' requires marking where AI content appears: P27.
units.anchor: specific sections of the article that use AI-generated content shall be identified
units.fit_note: Marks sections of an article, with a short explanation of the level of AI use, not code comments.

units.why: 'is common practice and, as such, is generally outside the intent of the above policy' exempts editing and grammar tools from the IEEE disclosure rule: P100.
units.anchor: is common practice and, as such, is generally outside the intent of the above policy

units.why: 'In this case, disclosure as noted above is recommended' says editing and grammar tool use should still be disclosed: P24.
units.anchor: In this case, disclosure as noted above is recommended.

units.why: 'Until formal advice is available use the Unpublished Material / Private Communication format' tells students how to cite AI in IEEE style: P25.
units.anchor: use the Unpublished Material / Private Communication format
units.fit_note: Gives a citation format for AI-generated content; it does not name tool, prompt or date.

units.why: 'An entry does not need to be included in the reference list' says an in-text citation alone is enough for AI as private communication: P24.
units.anchor: An entry does not need to be included in the reference list
units.fit_note: Says how much citation is needed; it does not require disclosure.

units.why: The page links 'Student AI Guide (2025)', pointing to further student guidance: P115.
units.anchor: Student AI Guide (2025)

notes: Coder A. Four included documents coded in full: utah-1 (2023 CTE post), utah-2 (AI & You Student Guide with six levels), utah-3 (CTE AI Tools for Education), utah-4 (ECE page). The ECE page is a department of electrical and computer engineering and its policy defers coursework AI to instructors. Sentences repeated across the CTE pages (syllabus statement, detector warnings) are coded again in each separate document; repeats inside one document were skipped.
